content: The Lloyds Bank coprolite, commonly referred to as the Lloyds Bank turd, is an exceptionally large piece of fossilized human feces. It was discovered in 1972 during an archaeological excavation of the Viking settlement of Jórvík, now modern-day York, England. The coprolite was unearthed beneath the site that would later become the York branch of Lloyds Bank. Remarkably, it is considered one of the largest known examples of fossilized human excrement ever found. Detailed analysis of this nine-inch (23 cm) long specimen revealed that its producer primarily consumed a diet consisting of meat and bread. Furthermore, the presence of several hundred parasitic eggs within the stool indicates that the individual suffered from a significant infestation of intestinal worms. In 1991, paleoscatologist Andrew Jones gained international attention when he appraised the coprolite for insurance purposes. He famously described it as the most exciting piece of excrement I've ever seen, adding that in its own way, it's as valuable as the Crown Jewels. The specimen was subsequently displayed at York's Archaeological Resource Centre, an educational and outreach institution operated by the York Archaeological Trust. Over the years, it captivated and fascinated generations of schoolchildren and visitors. Unfortunately, in 2003, the coprolite broke into three pieces after being accidentally dropped during an exhibition for a group of visitors. As of that year, efforts were underway to reconstruct and restore the specimen.
